AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT SALE OF UNSAFE TIRES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-195, to amend the Criminal Code (tire safety).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT SALE OF UNSAFE TIRES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT SALE OF UNSAFE TIRES
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to protect the public against unreasonable risk of highway accidents occurring as the result of motor vehicle tire failures. It would do this by an amendment to the Criminal Code which would prohibit any persons from manufacturing, selling or otherwise disposing of tires which might endanger the life or property of others. The governor in council will, by this proposal, establish and define safety standards for tires. I might say that this bill is similar to one adopted by the United States Senate.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

1.	Has any settlement been detected in the National Museum building and, if so (a) when was this first detected (b) what is the cause (c) has there been any increase in the settlement during the last year?
2.	What, if any, precautions have been taken to protect those who work in the museum and the visitors against injury caused by an abrupt or serious collapse of the building?
3.	Is the building, with any precautions now in effect, regarded as safe?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraith (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
1. Yes, (a) Even between 1906 and 1910, when this building was under construction, settlement was observed. By 1915 settlement was such that a portion of a high tower over the entrance was removed.
This is a massive structure. The exterior walls are heavily buttressed masonry bearing walls. The floors above the first floor level are carried on steel plate girders, simply supported and spanning from wall to wall. There is a complete basement and a partial sub-basement. The basement floor and the first floor are supported on a system of steelwork, simply supported and spanning from the exterior walls to interior cast iron columns, which in turn rest on the foundation walls of the subbasement. The footings supporting the exterior walls and the interior columns for the first floor are generally at two levels, approximately 12 feet and 22 feet below grade, (b) The site on which this building stands is not rigid. There is a stratum of man-made fill, about 8 to 10 feet in thickness, which is separated from bedrock by approximately 100 feet of soft sub-soil. This soil is subject to shrinking and swelling as the amount of water present in it varies. Moreover, the type of floor framing that was in practice at the time of the construction of the building is especially sensitive to differential settlements such as are observed in this building, (c) Where there has been slight total settlement in the past
Order for Return
year there has been no differential settlement which is the destructive force.
2.	Because of the problems caused by differential settlement during construction, the building has been under observation from time to time throughout its entire existence. These observations were intensified in 1958 when the Department of Public Works undertook a comprehensive engineering study of the structure. It was established that the basic structure was such that it was impractical to undertake changes to eliminate all the superficial damage caused by the differential settlement. It was decided the building should be checked regularly and this has been done. This inspection has been increased in the last year with the installation of special instrumentation for continuous observation of elevations and ground water levels. These are reviewed monthly and special examinations will be made should any construction activity take place on adjacent sites which could effect water levels.
The number of persons permitted in some areas has been limited. The number of persons in the auditorium, for example, has been limited to the number of permanent seats, i.e. 600. In addition, limits have been placed on the stack loads permitted in the library area. It is important to note that 95 per cent of the load on the footings is due to the weight of the structure and not to the weight of persons or materials occupying the building.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday my colleague, the hon. member for York South, dealt critically with the budget resolutions from the point of view of their impact upon any inequalities of income as between individuals within society, and also with the need to use fiscal policy as a tool for keeping the economy functioning. I wish to direct my remarks to a slightly different aspect of the problem. I want to refer to the impact of the resolutions on inequalities as between different regions of Canada.
My criticism of these resolutions will be that they and the policy they represent fail to take account of the need to level out regional inequalities. I need not remind members of the committee that one of the accepted economic purposes for government today is to iron out and eventually eliminate regional discrepancies or inequalities or inequities.
A balanced economic development of all areas of Canada was a goal which the Economic Council of Canada was directed to study. I am sure it is quite unnecessary to recall that that council in its second annual report, chapter 5, reviewed the question of regional growth and regional disparities. This chapter documents the persistent long-term disparities in economic growth, in income, in employment, in social services, and reveals that there is a substantial and long continued gap between the conditions in respect of these matters and the standards in these matters in some parts of Canada and other parts; and I refer particularly to the Atlantic provinces. I am aware that there have been set up a number of instruments of economic planning designed to deal with this very problem. The Atlantic Development Board, of course, is an illustration, and there are various provincial boards established and various

acts passed. Nevertheless, unless all the policies of government both federal and provincial are co-ordinated in a strategy of economic development, we will not achieve the goal of eliminating or ironing out these regional inequalities.
I should like to analyse the budget resolutions for a moment in order to show where I think they fall down. First of all, as I understand the policy which lies behind these budget resolutions it is that certain measures should be taken to cut back capital investment both private and public at the present time. As I understand it, and as explained by the minister, the reason for this is that in certain sections of our economy there is danger of overheating; that is, we have reached a stage in our expansion where there is virtual full employment and where there is a danger of inflation threatening the possibility of rising prices. Therefore certain steps were taken in these resolutions to damp down, as it were, the possible fires of inflation.
I should like to point out that this sort of a policy very well may make sense in parts of Canada but makes absolutely no sense in such areas as the Atlantic provinces where there is a 10 per cent rate of unemployment and where the urgent need is for more capital investment both public and private. I wonder whether the persons who advise the Minister of Finance are not able to devise some method to deal with this sort of problem without applying their policy to a section of the country in which there is certainly no need to dampen down the expansion but where there is every need to encourage investment. They should make sure that these measures do not apply in this area.
Paragraph 10 of the resolutions we are discussing deals with another matter which illustrates again the application of policies to Canada as a whole that make absolutely no sense in certain regions of the country. Although I do not wish to discuss paragraph 10 in detail now as I believe that will come up later, I do want to refer to the fact that paragraph 10 is designed to extend the incentives in the form of certain income tax exemptions for a further period. This applies to manufacturing or processing in designated areas. As we all know, this was discussed in the house the other day under the estimates of the Department of Industry and I shall not expand on it at any length because our views are known. The designated areas are defined by certain criteria which make perfectly good

sense, I suggest, generally speaking in respect of certain areas of the country, but they make absolutely no sense whatsoever in their application to the Atlantic provinces. I wish to refer to the eighth publication of the Atlantic pi'ovinces Economic Council. On several occasions that council has urged that the whole of the Atlantic region should be designated as an area for special assistance; yet, in the resolutions before us we have continued a designation based on a series of criteria which absolutely stand in the way of effective growth within the Atlantic provinces. It is true that this is under the Department of Industry Act, but it is made applicable by these resolutions.
I know of no economist who has studied this matter who does not agree that the whole of the Atlantic provinces, for example, should be a designated area. It makes absolutely no sense that areas of growth such as Halifax, Sydney, Saint John and Moncton-I name only the four which come to my mind at the moment-where there is a natural ability to develop economic growth should be excluded from the special incentives when we have been declaring it to be a matter of national policy to aid those areas of the country in which there is not adequate development and these are the very places in that area where the prospects of growth are most hopeful.
I pass on to another feature of our fiscal system which I suggest has exactly the same unfortunate effect. I refer to the way in which we obtain our tax for old age security. As hon. members know, this is at the rate of 4 per cent on the first $3,000 of taxable income up to a maximum of $120 a year. This tax is regressive. For all people whose income is above this amount the ceiling still is $120. When we consider the distribution of income as between regions in Canada we certainly should consider removing the regressive feature of this type of tax. In my view this tax is a relic of the age when it was considered as a source of revenue rather than as a means to regulate our economy and institute social policies.
When you have an area like the Atlantic provinces where incomes, as documented by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council report, are away below the average level this means that when you have this regressive type of taxation we are asking the people in the poorer regions of Canada to pay a larger portion of their incomes to finance old age security. If we are serious about ironing out

these inequities I suggest we should do something about this. I should like to say the same thing with regard to the Canada Pension Plan. This is all a part of the fiscal policy and tax structure. As I understand it, contributions to the Canada Pension Plan can be deducted for personal income tax purposes. The net result of this is that those with high incomes recover a great proportion of their contributions to this scheme. Because of the level of the tax they pay they get a higher percentage of benefit from the exemption that is granted while people at the lower income tax levels, on the other hand, get a lesser benefit.

This makes it extremely difficult for the small wage earner who owns his own home or is buying it to make ends meet. At the municipal level he finds himself taxed heavily for education. Approximately 50 per cent of his taxes at the municipal level goes for education, and he is allowed no income tax deduction in this regard. He does not get any income tax deduction for the interest on his mortgage payments. If something is not done for these people, there will be no incentive to own property. As a matter of fact, there will not be much incentive to work. When you add to all this the 10 per cent hike in food costs last year you get a rather dreary and dismal picture for these people.
I should like to ask the minister if he does not think this is one of the causes of the labour unrest across Canada. People are being pinched because they have not got
June 8, 1966

enough to make ends meet, so in self-defence they go out on strike. I should like to ask the minister if he has given any consideration to that problem. I think it is a No. 1 priority.
I should like to say a few words now about the regional discrepancies in pay and costs of living across Canada. These remarks apply not only to people who earn their incomes in these areas and pay their taxes but they also apply very pointedly to the old age pensioners. I wonder just how these people are living on $75 per month. I should like to remind the minister that about 70 per cent of the ladies of this country who are 70 and over and about 60 per cent of the men have no other income but the pension. I say to the minister that, with taxes and inflation, this is tragic.
I should like to say a few words about the 5 per cent corporate tax on businesses earning over $30,000. In my opinion this tax will increase the cost of production and the prices of the products these corporations are selling. I believe this is a vital matter because our productivity now is only about two-thirds of that of the country to the south of us. We have to meet world competition. I wonder about the paradox of this situation and I should like the minister to think about it.
I am not critical of the designation of incentive areas across Canada because it does create employment. But how in the world does the minister square the fact that on the one hand he offers an incentive of up to 20 per cent of capital costs and accelerated write-offs to business going into these areas while on the other hand he puts a 5 per cent tax on the corporate income of those business firms that are already producing and meeting competition in world markets? The only thing I can say to the minister is that in my opinion this is a complete paradox. He imposes a tax to hold some corporations back and slow down inflation while on the other hand he goes around offering incentives to other corporations which creates inflation. What sort of paradox is this?
I want to go a little further and comment on the idea of giving back the money from the 5 per cent tax to these corporations in 18 to 24 months. I think the minister is a real sharp financier because at the present rate of erosion of the dollar-it was 4 per cent last year-he is going to clip the amount down to the point where they will not be getting their 5 per cent. I ask the minister to take another look at the $145 million he hopes to raise by this method.
Income Tax Act
In conclusion I should like to make a suggestion to the minister. In formulating the rules and directions for preparing income tax returns the department should make them simple enough that the ordinary man can interpret them. We have rules and instructions now which the ordinary taxpayer cannot interpret. He has to get a specialist to interpret them. Surely this wrong should be corrected. The people we work for should be able to interpret the rules that we lay down.

I believe it should be apparent to the Minister of Finance by now, Mr. Chairman, that the members of the New Democratic Party have been examining the proposals he has put forward in the income tax resolution from two points of view. On the one hand, we have been concerned about the extent to which the income tax proposals are being utilized as a tool for economic planning. On the other hand, we have been concerned about whether and to what extent the income tax proprosals move in the direction of achieving social justice through an appropriate restructuring and amendment of the Income Tax Act. I have some comments I should like to make about the income tax resolution from both those points of view.
I listened to my colleague, the hon. member for Greenwood, a short time ago suggesting that the proposals of the minister are inadequate in relation to furthering the appropriate regional expansion in Canada, particularly from the point of view of those areas where the rate of economic growth is by all counts completely inadequate.
I happen to come from a part of Canada which has been expanding at a very rapid rate, particularly in the primary industries which lie in the area of my constituency. In recent years I have sometimes had the feeling that one could expect an announcement of a new, multi-million dollar pulp mill expansion or building project almost every other week. Certainly some of the corporations that have been engaged in this form of activity have been showing a very handsome profit picture and will be among those corporations in Canada that will be affected by the minister's so-called refundable tax proposal. I share the views of my colleagues that the minister's gesture is a very feeble and halting one. It is not designed to overcome in any way what I consider to be the very serious disparity of growth within my own area. I am referring to the disparity of growth between industrial plant and the necessary community facilities

that should go with the growth of industry so that the people who are going to provide the work force can enjoy the normal amenities of modern life.

In my view, if the sort of move the minister is proposing in this tax, which has been discussed in some detail by the hon. member for Greenwood and earlier by the hon. member for York South, is to have any real effect for the benefit and welfare of the people of Canada, one of its purposes should be to assist in ensuring that along with industrial growth goes the necessary and proper expansion of the normal community facilities which enable people to live and raise and educate their children.
It seems to me that far from taking into account this aspect of growth in our country the government has in another proposal moved completely in the opposite direction. The only announced public policy in this field is the cut-back of 10 per cent in government spending in its own construction program. This, particularly in areas where there is rapid economic growth and expansion, can and does result in very real hardship to the people who are asked to go and live and work in these areas. In an area along the seacoast such as mine the necessary public wharves, seaplane landing floats and all those facilities which come under the responsibility of the federal government must be provided to keep pace with the needs of the people and industry of the area.
In the field of housing-if the Minister of Labour were here he could verify that I have had some rather extensive discussions with him with respect to the proper expansion of housing facilities-the policies which have been followed under the direction of the Minister of Labour and the government as a whole have resulted in the basic disparity between economic industrial expansion and the provision of housing and related facilities becoming worse and worse.
If the Minister of Finance, in his use of income tax as an economic tool, had made some provision in his proposals to redress the balance between the kind of expenditures that large corporations are able to make apparently at will in order to build new pulp mills and other plants of that kind, or to develop overnight very large mining operations to ship iron ore to Japan, by redirecting the funds that the minister suggests should be withdrawn from these corporations to the

provision of a balanced growth in areas like those to be found in many parts of British Columbia, I for one would have been a much happier member in rising to discuss the minister's income tax proposals.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn my attention to the other aspect of the proposals which, as I have suggested, is a major one so far as the members of the New Democratic Party are concerned.
I am going to bring to the attention of the minister an example of what I consider to be a complete ignoring of a basic injustice in the present income tax structure. It is a basic injustice which divides the people of Canada according to the particular form in which they receive their income.
As the Income Tax Act now stands there is built into it a dividing line which discriminates against the vast majority of Canadians whose source of income is from salary or wages. I have quoted in the past many examples of this situation. As a matter of fact, I believe I have raised this question in every budget discussion while I have been a member of the house. I cannot recall whether I raised it when Hon. Douglas Abbott was minister of finance but I certainly did on several occasions when Hon. Walter Harris was the minister. At least two ministers of finance of the Conservative administration also heard from me about the matter. Last year I raised it in the house when the hon. member for Davenport was minister of finance and he went as far as saying that he would have a look at the matter.
So far as public statements in the house are concerned the matter is not as far advanced as it was when Mr. Harris presented his last Budget. It had been completely ignored for a number of years but Mr. Harris publicly admitted on the floor of the house that discrimination did exist in this area and that he and his department were prepared to take a look at it.
I could cite a number of examples of such discrimination but I will cite only one. Most members of the Canadian medical profession are in private practice. They are not on salaries or wages, though many men in that profession, of course, do draw their income in that way. If I understand correctly the application of the present Income Tax Act, a medical man in private practice who wishes to purchase certain medical textbooks to assist him in the carrying on of his work is quite properly able to deduct the expense from his taxable income. On the other hand,
June 8, 1966

Income Tax Act
if a medical man is in a salaried job and needs the same textbooks he is not able to deduct the cost of the books from his gross income for income tax purposes.
In my submission this is a problem which applies much more broadly to people who are engaged in the teaching profession, almost all of whom are working and receiving their income in the form of salaries or wages. For that matter, the textbooks required by students at universities and other schools are not considered to be expense items deductible for income tax purposes.
One could cite other examples, Mr. Chairman. I have raised many times one aspect of this matter which affect a great many people in my constituency. I refer to workers who are engaged in the type of employment which requires them to travel in the course of their work from their regular place of residence to camps where they live and pay board and also incur travel expenses in going to and from their homes from time to time. Various occupational groups are particularly concerned, such as miners and loggers. Fishermen are not too much affected because for income tax purposes most fishermen are classified as self-employed and do indeed enjoy benefits under the Income Tax Act which are denied other workers.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In this connection I should like to remind the house that this longstanding discrimination was aggravated in 1957 when the former member for Eglinton presented his first budget. Because of a particular situation that had developed in the preceding parliament he saw fit to introduce an amendment to section 5 of the Income Tax Act providing for specific exemptions for certain classes of workers who have to travel. I refer, of course, to the amendment providing exemptions for those who are engaged in the construction field.
I suggest that in section 11, subsection 5, of the Income Tax Act there is an example-and I am not quarreling that this exemption is allowed-is to be found of another particular group or class of employees whose incomes derive from wages or salaries and whose expenses incurred in a certain way may be deducted from such incomes. This is the provision that refers to people who are employed by railway companies. It allows them to deduct expenses for meals and lodging while they are from their normal places of residence.
It seems to me, if we are to move toward achieving social justice in the application of
income tax, that it is not good enough to pick out a particular group now and then and provide the kind of exemption to which I have referred. It does not matter whether you pick out railway workers, construction workers or others.
In 1956 the Liberal minister of finance stood up in the house, admitted that discrimination existed under the act and said that he was prepared to look at it. The present Minister of Finance has not been in office too long. I do not know what opportunity he has had to examine this question. Perhaps he has been preoccupied with his famous 5 per cent refundable corporation tax.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal for a few moments with the changes in the first paragraph of the resolution. In doing so I must agree with the hon. member for Simcoe East that these changes, the increase in relation to certain tax brackets and the decrease in respect of others, have not eased the pressure. We must ask what is really the purpose behind these changes. Was it to produce more revenue? For an answer we may have to refer to the minister's own words at the time he made his Budget statement.
Consider the labour situation. We have problems today with the longshoremen, with employees of the Canadian National Railways and with employees of Trans-Canada Air Lines. In fact there is trouble right down the road. Surely this is all due basically to the high cost of living which the budget did nothing to cure. In my opinion inflation is still rampant. The wage earners find that they are taking home less pay because of increases in taxation. In addition, of course, the purchasing power of their wages has declined. I notice that today the dollar is worth only 37J cents compared with its value at the end of the war. This is the main reason we have all these troubles.
The minister said he made these tax changes so as to curb inflation. The Globe and Mail had this to say:
Finance Minister Mitchell Sharp was at pains to explain that his budget was designed to slow down but not to halt the boom, to reduce the inflation factor in the increase in the gross national product, to steady the headlong Canadian course by cutting the amount of money individuals and business would have to send chasing after a short supply of labour and materials.
The Globe and Mail goes on to say that the whole trend of the minister's remarks was to indicate the need for restraint. That was the keynote of his message. But restraint by whom?
June 8, 1966

The hon. gentleman is seeking to ensure by these changes that the consumers spend less money. So far as labour and materials are concerned I do not believe there is any shortage in this country. The big shortage in Canada today is money. What did the government intend to do? The minister said that the budget was designed to curb inflation and hold the cost of living steady. But it has done nothing in this regard. The purpose which the minister was trying to achieve through taxing individuals has been upset by the government itself, because the government intends this year to spend 9.6 per cent more money than in 1965-66. In that year the budget totalled $7,707 million. For 1966-67 it was increased to $8.5 billion, an increase of almost 10 per cent. In other words, the government is saying to individuals that though it intends to spend more they shall have less to spend on consumer goods as part of an attempt to control the boom.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the boom is a fiction because if one goes into the average home owned by an average wage earner or small farmer or businessman one finds that he is suffering today as he suffered in the recession of the thirties because of less money to spend on consumer goods and the necessities of life. The budget has done nothing to help in this regard.
The minister talks about tax cuts. What did these cuts amount to? For the bulk of the people, for the 60 per cent of our taxpayers who pay 88 per cent of all the income tax, the tax bill will be higher. Th's section includes those who are on strike today or who are about to go on strike with an adverse affect on the whole picture of gross national production. I say this because the Canadian Wheat Board admits we have lost contracts for 30 million bushels of grain. The board takes a much more serious view of this matter than the minister under whose responsibility it comes. Indeed, the officials say now that the loss may amount to 75 million bushels. Meanwhile the government is accepting no responsibility to assist the nation in getting this grain market.
It is not only the farmers of western Canada who are affected. The longshoremen's strike is damaging the whole economy of the nation. In my opinion this budget was a straight bluff. It did noting to curb inflation. The blame for what has happened lies on the shoulders of the present government. No explanation is ever given us of what these resolutions mean. What do they mean? I have
Income Tax Act
pointed out that more than half our taxpayers will have to pay more. What about the others? To a man with a wife and two children earning $4,000 a year, which is above the average as the minister knows, this so-called tax cut means $3 a year, which amounts to nothing when one considers the cost of living today. This is why we have strikes on the Great Lakes and on the St. Lawrence. This is why we will have a strike at Air Canada and in various other places -trouble everywhere, in fact. If this government could be labelled and given a new name it might well be called the government of trouble and crisis. Hon. gentlemen opposite are not measuring up to their responsibilities.
We on this side of the house continually put questions to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. We get no answers. What did the minister say with reference to the wheat situation? He said it was very serious. Yesterday I asked him a simple question. I asked him whether the strike would affect the contracts we have with Russia and other nations. In reply he said: Well, it is going to be serious. But when the officials of the Canadian Wheat Board appeared before the committee they told us what the facts really were.
The minister has removed a tax cut given by his predecessor before the government went to the people. He would have us believe he is reducing the tax for those in the lower income brackets. But this so-called reduction amounts to only $3 a year and will have no effect whatever on the cost of living. Yet the cost of living is the biggest problem facing parliament today. I say the Minister of Finance has failed in his responsibility to curb inflation and that his budget has done nothing in this regard.
The leading newspapers of this nation, the Globe and Mail, the Winnipeg Free Press, the Calgary Herald and other papers in western Canada, all agree that the budget did nothing to curb inflation or prevent the cost of living from rising further. I see hon. members on the other side looking at me while I am speaking. They know, as I do, that the biggest volume of mail crossing our desks today as members of parliament is mail complaining about the high cost of living. In my opinion this is the reason the former minister of finance was fired. He was not fired because he recommended the calling of an election which did not work out very well. He was fired because his policies were aggravating the situation.

If the minister reads Hansard he will see what I and other opposition members said about the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan. We pointed out that the plan and the manner in which it was brought in would only aggravate inflation. Today every small business firm has to employ one person for every other five people just for the purpose of keeping government records. That in itself has increased overhead costs.
On top of that employers are paying more tax. They pay Canada Pension Plan contributions for their employees. Professional men have been forced to increase their fees and small businessmen have raised their prices. Thus the spiralling rise in the cost of living continues.
Despite all this the government refuses to produce any concrete policy. It would rather have the country believe that the opposition obstructs. My answer to that is that the government has never brought in those pieces of legislation that would have helped cure our economic problems. The government is scared to bring in the amendments to the Bank Act because of political sensitivity.
Cabinet ministers wanted to govern and wanted responsibility. They said so during the election. Why don't they accept that responsibility? We cannot be charged with obstruction when we have never had any serious legislation to obstruct. The government is sitting on all legislation that would

help the situation and which parliament could examine. It is hoping that something may happen between now and an adjournment so that the political sensitivity will die down.
From what I read in the newspapers about leakages from the Liberal caucus I know that the Minister of Finance is concerned. In the caucus there is a group led by the former minister of finance and the present minister has his own group. The two groups cannot come together on amendments to the Bank Act and changes in the Income Tax Act.
There is trouble in the government and in the Liberal ranks. Government supporters know it. I see two of them smiling. They are probably wondering where I get my information but what I am telling them is absolutely correct. One does not even have to read the papers. Sometimes when you go up and down in the elevators you get a free bit of information from the Liberals themselves.
Liberal members are sitting around in their offices wondering which minister of finance they should support, and the Prime Minister is the biggest juggler. When he makes a speech you do not know whether he is supporting the former minister or the present minister, both of whom are politically ambitious and are looking to the throne of the Prime Minister with envious eyes.
The main problem today besides the cost of living is the shortage of money. The little man who wants to buy a home cannot get a dollar on a mortgage. In the city of Calgary, and I am sure the same is true in many other cities, people are paying interest rates as high as 12 and 15 per cent because the government will not introduce amendments to the Bank Act. The government has tightened the money supply just as the Liberals did in 1956. There is no money for small people to carry on business. Contractors are going broke. Housing is a problem, and it is all because the government will not face up to its responsibility. In particular it is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance.
I say kindly to the minister that if his cabinet colleagues are so timid and will not do the things that are necessary it is up to him to tell them: I am a man who likes to show that I accept my responsibilities and will take action. If his colleagues will not go along with him then, the minister knows the decision he must take, and it may be the same decision as the former minister. Because of tight money some contractors cannot complete apartment block buildings.

I wish the minister of northern affairs were in the chamber. I was told by an official whom I cannot and must not name that in our national parks on some nights last year there were more than a thousand people who could not get accommodation. One reason for that is the tight money policy of the government and another is that it has taken away from these people security of tenure in the land on which they operate with the result that they cannot borrow what they need.
There is trouble everywhere on the labour and management scenes. Some of that trouble could be solved if the minister would stand up to his own colleagues. These income tax changes mean nothing. They merely undo what was done last year when the Liberals tried to get a majority and failed. As I pointed out, the reduction in taxes means an additional $3 a year to throw around.
The minister should go to Safeway and find out the price of beef today. It is $1 a pound.

I am tired of sitting in my place and hearing people talk in circles. Let us deal in dollars and cents. On that basis I say the government is a failure. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I proceed to deal with these two amendments which I should like to have made to paragraphs 7 and 14 of the resolution. First, on paragraph 7, which deals with stock options, the proposal that was made in the budget to withdraw part of the extremely generous features of the existing formula has given rise to some protest from interested employees. Broadly speaking these protest have concentrated on three points. First, it is urged that some tax concession should be granted to provide incentives to key employees; second, it is urged that Canada should not tax special benefits more severely than similar benefits are taxed in the United States; third, it is claimed that the proposed change is retroactive in effect.
On the first of these points, there has been a fairly prevalent view that the holding of stock by employees, particularly key employees, is an incentive to their putting in their best efforts on behalf of the company. However, the proposition that special low rates of tax should be provided for certain forms of remuneration of employees in order to provide incentives for greater effort has not to my knowledge been advanced in a serious way before.
The tax system has been used to provide incentives for business and perhaps it could be used to provide rewards and incentives for employees but any tax provision for this purpose would have to be both fair and effective and I question whether it should be left entirely to employers to select the beneficiaries of such a scheme as it is under the present arrangement for stock option plans.
On the point that stock options should not be taxed more heavily in Canada than in the United States, the present Canadian formula taxes these benefits in some cases at a rate much less than in the United States even though in that country such benefits are taxed at the long-term capital gains rate of 25 per cent if they conform with the rule?

governing qualified stock option plans or employee stock purchase plans. A qualified stock option cannot be issued at less than the market value of the stock when the option was issued. These assertions raise the whole question of what is retroactive legislation. I believe that to change the rate of tax on income already received would be retroactive but surely no taxpayer has justification for expecting that the rate of personal income tax on his income will not be changed. An individual who enters into a contract of employment, or a business that enters into a business undertaking expecting a certain rate of return, cannot be assured that rates of income tax will remain unchanged during the term of that contract or business undertaking.
This point, and I should like to stress this, may have significance in the months ahead. It is to be expected that the report of the royal commission soon to be received will recommend changes in our tax laws. Mr. Chairman, my understanding is that we are dealing with the whole of this resolution, and I thought it might help in the consideration of the resolution if there were formally before the committee at this stage the proposed amendments that I would like to have moved at an appropriate time. These are quite important to the discussion of the whole matter. I have no objection, of course, to what the Leader of the Opposition said, namely, to a general discussion upon any part of the resolution. I believe that is quite appropriate.
May I then deal with what I will propose as amendments to paragraph 14. This is the

paragraph dealing with the 5 per cent refundable tax on corporations. In the Budget speech I referred to the fact that this was a novel measure and I said I would welcome constructive suggestions concerning the application of the tax. I am pleased to report that I have received a number of comments and suggestions. These have been very helpful and they have all been examined with great care. Although I have not found it possible to accept all of these suggestions there are several modifications which I would like to recommend to the committee. I should add that these modifications are of a kind that would not normally be discussed at the resolution stage but would be left to be incorporated in the bill. However, since the resolution described this tax in conciderable detail and since there is widespread interest in these details, I think it would be preferable to make these changes known now. The simplest way to do this seems to be by amending the resolution. The changes proposed are all to paragraph 14. I have now distributed to hon. members the text of what I will have moved at an appropriate time.
It will be noted that the amendment is in three parts or paragraphs. Paragraph (a) proposes that three types of investment company, and also charitable trusts, be made exemp from the tax. The first kind of investment company referred to is an investment company described in section 69 of the Income Tax Act. The companies described in section 69 are often called investment funds or mutual funds. These companies or funds are widely used by individuals who seek to diversify their investments. These companies must operate in a certain way in order to qualify for the special provisions of section 69. For example, at least 95 per cent of their income must be from investments, 85 per cent of gross revenue must be from sources in Canada, and 85 per cent of income after taxes must be distributed each year. It is considered that this kind of company, which is merely a conduit for receiving investment income, should not be made subject to the special 5 per cent tax.
I might add that mutual investment funds operated through a trust instead of through a corporation will not have any amount subject to the tax unless they receive rents or conduct a business. Interest and dividends received by such a trust would not be considered business income.
The second kind of investment company referred to is a non-resident owned invest-
June 8, 1966

ment company, usually called by my officials, to my great confusion, an NRO. These companies are established by non-residents to hold investments in Canada. If they conform with the rules found in section 70 of the act they pay a special rate of tax of 15 per cent which is, in effect, a prepayment of the non-resident withholding tax. These companies are also merely conduits for receiving investment income. Moreover, they will receive dividends from other Canadian companies which have borne the special 5 per cent tax. It seems reasonable that this kind of company should not be subject to the 5 per cent tax.
The third kind of investment company referred to is also wholly owned by non-residents. These are companies which have little or no property in Canada and which do not invest in Canada. They are companies which collect dividends and interest from various parts of the world and forward this investment income to their non-resident shareholders. It would not be in keeping with the purposes of the 5 per cent tax to include these companies.
The charitable trusts which this part of the amendment would exempt are described in section 62 (1) (g) of the Income Tax Act. These trusts must meet certain requirements, including one which prohibits them from carrying on a business. Since charitable corporations described in this section of the act are to be exempt it is considered reasonable that charitable trusts, which are very similar, should also be exempt.

Mr. Chairman, I will not speak at length at this late hour. I have listened to the speeches made by the hon. member for Simcoe East and the hon. member for Bow River. They placed before the house the thinking of the average Canadian. The fabulous increases in expenditure by this government after its promises of economy are becoming more and more apparent in the degree to which this government has gone on a spending spree.
I will not go into other details this afternoon except to refer to one example which is a perfect commentary on the wastefulness of this government. I am referring to the undertaking, which is now apparently in the embryonic stage, of building in the city of Ottawa a $100 million pentagon building which, by the time it is completed, having regard to the way costs are going up, will cost the Canadian people $125 million to $150 million. There can be no excuse for this expenditure. Certainly improvements can be made in the housing for those engaged in defence and in the defence department but this is an example of the degree to which this government has lost all sense of proportion. Tax, tax, and spend, spend.
The whole concept consists of a tremendous venture. Someone suggested today it will be built of white stone. If it is, it may well earn the appellation of "Canada's white elephant".
I cannot conceive, with taxes being raised as they are now being raised by this government to being the highest level in peacetime history and at a time of the greatest cost of living in peace or war, that a government should engage in this type of self-glorification. Originally it was intended that the building should cost $35 million.

What we want is somebody to dominate the thinking of this government and convince it that this type of expenditure, whether it is $30 million or $50 million, is not justified. Across this nation there are people who find it difficult to carry on in the face of the increasing cost of living in respect of which no action has been taken. Yet the image created by this government is that no matter how ridiculous the plan may be the Canadian people shall continue to be taxed in order to meet its grandiose conceptions. An example of this attitude of mind was shown by the Secretary of State when she flew a kite to ascertain whether or not Canadians were sufficiently artistically-minded to accept paying $6 million for a painting to be placed in the national gallery. Whether it is $35 million or $50 million or whatever the amount of expenditure for the building in question may be, this is no time for the glorification of the minister of defence by such an expenditure. subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMPENSATION FOR DEPENDANTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the expediency of introducing legislation for the creation of a criminal injuries compensation board to hear the pleas of persons who have suffered permanent injury or disability as the victims of crime and award compensation to such persons or their dependants as would seem fair in the circumstances, and wherever possible to do so, to impose payment of compensation by criminals to those they have injured.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is private members' hour and as the word "hour" indicates that is the length of time that will be devoted
June 8, 1966

to this question. I do not intend to speak at length because I should like to see this motion come to a vote today so that the cabinet can be advised of the feeling of the House of Commons on the matter enunciated in the notice of motion. As a private member it is impossible for me to introduce a bill involving the expenditure of public moneys.
The only way to draw the cabinet's attention to the fact that we are desirous of seeing a compensation fund established so that the victims of criminals can be compensated for injuries that they or their dependants suffer is to introduce a notice of motion advising the cabinet that they should consider the expediency of introducing legislation for the creation of a criminal injuries compensation board. This notice of motion was entered on the order paper on January 20, two days after the house met in January of this year. Five days of the time of this house were devoted to a discussion of the abolition of capital punishment, three in March and two in April. Those five days can be described as days devoted to seeking an improvement in the lot of the criminal element in the nation. Only a minimum of time was spent in discussing the fate of the victims of murderers.
This motion has been brought forward by the retentionists, as they are called, in order to show that there are people in this nation who are sympathetic to the victims of murders, homicides and manslaughters and are sympathetic to the dependants and relatives of those victims. The way the state rushes to provide psychiatrists to examine everyone accused of murder and rushes to see that they are given most comfortable surroundings while awaiting trial, it does seem that the state is willing to spend money on behalf of the criminal but has not given any thought to the victim. I am sorry to state that I have some personal knowledge of a number of murders in the city of Toronto where I was not only connected with a large newspaper but was a member of a large congregation. The fact that the victim of murder is not given any consideration by the state is very upsetting to millions of people in the Dominion of Canada.
I am thinking of a little seven year old girl in our Sunday school who was murdered one Tuesday evening by a man in his early twenties. He has been ajudged insane. He is going to spend the rest of his life in an asylum at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers, having three meals a day, comfortable quarters and a comfortable bed. No doubt
Criminal Injuries Compensation Board within eight or ten years the parole board will find that his sanity has been restored and he will be released into society after many thousands of dollars have been spent in his behalf. What has the state done for the little seven year old girl? I happen to know that the public school which the little doll attended started a fund to aid the family at the time of their distress and collected a total of $191. This included $75 from Victoria Presbyterian Church where the little girl attended Sunday school. Other people went to work and collected a fund on behalf of the family. I am happy to state that many people sent in contributions, having heard on the radio or read in the newspapers about the dastardly crime. A few thousand dollars were contributed to the relief of the family.
This was a voluntary effort. Nothing was contributed by the state in any manner, shape or form. The state was far too busy providing a defence in the way of psychiatric examination and all that for the accused; they had no time for the little girl. Hon. members may recall the two policemen who were shot in Montreal. Of course, their relatives would be eligible for compensation from the policemen's compensation fund. We had a case of a policeman in Toronto, McQuillan, who was shot and killed by a man about 20 years ago. He also was a member of Victoria Presbyterian Church. In this case the policeman's family was able to draw compensation from the policemen's injury and death fund.
What about those people who are not policemen and who are killed? What about their families? I do not need to give a long recitation about the families where murders have been committed and the breadwinner has been lost. In many cases the widow has to go to work to support the children because no compensation is given for the loss of the breadwinner. In some provinces she immediately becomes eligible for mother's allowance, but no particular compensation is given because the breadwinner has been shot down in cold blood.
It is ridiculous to think of the time and energy that the state spends looking after the best interests of the criminal and seeing that he gets a fair trial. If he cannot pay for a lawyer himself, then the state provides a lawyer. In all cases the expenses are paid by the state, by you and by me, by all of us including the family of the victim of the murder because they are taxpayers too.
We have the case of Trans-Canada Air Lines

Criminal Injuries Compensation Board -if my French speaking friends do not like that name then I will say Air Canada so they will understand what I am talking about- which is an arm of the government We have to pay the deficits of that air line. When they have a crash, as they did at Ste. Therese de Blainville or as they did at Armstrong about 20 years ago or when a plane disappeared west of Vancouver and has never been seen since, compensation is paid to the families of the victims of these air crashes. The airplane can be considered an arm of the government. However, there is no compensation for the victims of murderers.
Let us consider the case of the Canadian National Railways, which is an arm of the government or a crown corporation, if you wish. If there are deficits the Canadian taxpayer has to pay them. If people are killed as the result of negligence on the part of C.N.R. employees, by being run down at railroad crossings or as passengers on trains who are killed as a result of the negligent operation of the train, they can collect from the Canadian National Railways.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I am glad to say that in most provinces today there are workmen's compensation funds. If a workman is killed in the course of his duties compensation is paid to his family out of provincial funds so that the family will not immediately be placed on welfare and have to live on handouts from people filled with compassion. The state looks after families whose breadwinner is killed in the course of his work through the medium of the workmen's compensation fund.
As another example, if a person is run down by a motor car on the highways of the nation his family can sue the person who caused his death or injury. If they cannot collect from the person who caused his death or injury because that person has no insurance or no means, then resort may be had to the unsatisfied judgment fund which is maintained by the provincial governments for such cases. If a person is killed by a car his family has a means of redress; if the same person is killed by a murderer no compensation from the state is provided his family.
In discussing this matter only yesterday with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) we were smiling over the fact that, under the dog tax and sheep protection act of the province of Ontario, if a farmer loses sheep because dogs get into his pen and destroy them that farmer can

DEBATES	June 8. 1966
collect compensation for the loss of his sheep. But if the hired hand murders the farmer's daughter, as happened recently at Dublin, Ontario, which is between Stratford and Goderich, then the farmer has no claim unless he wants to sue the murderer's family. But who wants the families of victims such as this to have to go to court and prolong the agony associated with a murder in their family?
By the way, Mr. Speaker, the Dublin case is interesting in view of all the hullabaloo and uproar raised by the Truscott matter. The Truscott affair occurred at Clinton. The murder of the farmer's daughter by the former hired hand occurred at Dublin, Ontario, which is only 10 or 15 miles from Clinton. There is hardly anybody who is seeking to abolish capital punishment who cares about Lynne Harper, the girl murdered at Clinton, or about the farmers' daughter shot dead at Dublin.
If a car leaves the highway and crashes through a fence and kills a cow or a pig, the farmer can collect compensation from the driver if he goes to court about the matter. But whoever heard of a father, mother, wife, brother or sister collecting compensation through the courts because someone near and dear to them had been killed by a murderer?
I do not wish to talk at length on this matter. I believe the subject matter in itself carries conviction. I should like to see the House of Commons support this motion so that the cabinet will know that the people of Canada wish them to establish such a compensation fund to relieve the families of murdered victims, or victims of other crimes in the future. I sincerely trust that this matter will come to a vote today.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMPENSATION FOR DEPENDANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is a most challenging motion which has been brought before the house by the hon. member. It has always seemed strange to me, both while I served in the Royal
June 8, 1966

Canadian Mounted Police and as an ex-member of that force, that in the division between civil law and criminal law a man who is responsible for negligence involving monetary assessment is not responsible in cases of murder, deliberate assault or, as was often the case, grievous bodily harm. In the case of murder, of course, his act ended in the death of the breadwinner of a family.
I think that this oversight, which is historical and of long standing, is probably due to the fact that at one time felons who were guilty of such crimes as murder, grievous assault, robbery and certain other crimes against the state forfeited all of their property automatically to the crown. In those days the poor, were not looked after except through the largesse of the king. Naturally there was no point in fining the criminal because he had no property anyway. So the crown undertook responsibility for looking after victims, if indeed they were looked after at all.
I think there is a great deal of merit in the idea that compensation should be paid to people who have suffered personal injury or have lost money due to felonies committed against them. I am not sure that the hon. member has the right answer when he says that we should set up another board. It seems to me that with a fairly simple section inserted in our criminal law we could give a judge the power to assess against a criminal's estate the full amount necessary to compensate the victim or victims of the offence to the extent that the estate was able to pay. Some action of that kind I feel is necessary.
There is another way to bring about the objective of the motion which the house might like to consider. I think that if criminals are not hanged-apparently they are not; most of them are kept in jail for a certain length of time-they should be paid for work they do in the penitentiary and should be assessed the full amount of the monetary consequences of their crime by way of compensation. Some people do not mind going to jail. Jails today are fairly comfortable compared with the medieval institutions which used to exist. There is television, the men are given a ration of cigarettes, some of them work in the library and others in the flower garden. Their feelings are always taken into consideration and they can have a pretty decent time in jail today. I think that we should strike a happy medium between the punitive side of imprisonment and the justice
Criminal Injuries Compensation Board aspect. Certainly I do not think that all of the consideration should be given to the criminal.
I agree with the hon. member that the person who is the object of the crime should be considered first. The person who has been hurt should at least be considered equally with the person who has committed the wrong. I think it would be more than just to reduce penalties to the lowest common denominator, good old money, something for which every human being I have met has considerable respect.
You would reach a criminal's conscience psychologically provided he knew that if he committed a crime and was caught and brought to justice he would not only spend a few months in a comfortable jail watching television and planning his next crime but would also go to work, labour productively, even if only on the good old rock pile, and be paid $1.25 an hour, the minimum federal wage. He would not get rich because I would have him pay back to society every cent he owed, including the amount which the judge considered he owed the people he had wronged.
There would be nothing unfair about this method. We would not have to say that we thought he had done a day's work. We are living in the age of electronic computers, and he would be able to push a loaded wheelbarrow over an electronic scale and the value of the number of tons of dirt he had shovelled or the number of tons of rock he had crushed would be credited to his account. Before he left the penal institution he would be forced to pay in full the exact amount involved in his crime. Going back to the good old Gilbert and Sullivan solution to the problem I say, let the punishment fit the crime.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Most crimes boil down to dollars and cents. Robberies in which violence is involved stem from greed. I do not think there could be anything better psychologically-psychology is as old as the jungle-than making criminals understand that when they break into an old widow's home and steal the savings she has put away in her tea pot they will have to pay. If you run over a widow with a motor car on the highway the civil law of the land will make you pay damages. If you have a flat tire and your car skids into her the civil court will still hold you responsible for her damages. Surely if the damages to such a woman are intentional those damages ought to be made good. The court ought to allow her a good holiday in Bermuda.

In Alberta there was a case where a couple of men sawed off an old man's legs with a hacksaw. They picked up $20. If the law were amended as I should like to see it amended, that would be the most expensive fifteen minutes fun such men would ever have. The old victim ought to be given two years in Bermuda or any other island of his choice. I expect he would like to get away from Alberta in the winter. The criminals would pay for the plane fare and the holiday. There would be no tiger in the tank handout because the holiday would be awarded as a matter of right.
The criminal would not decide how many tons of dirt he would have to move because this would be decided for him by the electronic wheelbarrow. Some of these young fellows today play it hard because we play it soft. They might say they were not going to work, but I have some news for them. Everything would be voluntary. They would have to pay for their board and go to a commissariat as we had to do in the army. If you wanted a beer for 2d you got a beer for 2d. If you wanted a better beer you had to pay more. If these young men wanted a T-bone steak they would have to pay $2.75 for it. To earn that much they would have to wheel so many tons of sand or dirt over the electronic scale. But if they do not want to work there is no need for them to starve. They can always go to the cookhouse and get a bowl of lukewarm mush flavoured with iodine and all sorts of vitamins to keep a man alive, which would be very distasteful. The bones of such a man who has eaten the mush would meet the full approval of the medical profession because all the necessary vitamins would be present. If the man works he gets $1.25 an hour. If he does not work he gets nothing. Should the man decide to work, he should be given a decent bed with white sheets and pushbutton television at two bits an hour. On the other hand, if he decides not to work he sleeps on a straw tick. We had those in the army and they were fine. We did not see anything wrong with them. They were called straw palliasses. They are nice and soft. You do not get lumbago from them because they keep your back straight. If a man slept on one he would wait until the temperature got to 49 degrees Fahrenheit, when he would be shivering just a little bit, before getting a blanket. If he wanted to return to work he would get the $1.25 an hour and the nice, comfortable bed.

I have only had 23 years experience with these people and I know that they appreciate justice. They do not like unpleasant people who do not treat them nicely. They appreciate justice and they could not argue with the computer. Their wages would be paid in direct proportion to the amount of dirt they moved. I believe that if we set up such a camp the criminal population, especially the repeaters in our penal institutions, would be reduced to zero. These people cannot stand justice.
I think it is high time we took a new look at criminology, penology and the rest of the "ologies", and came back to good old-fashioned common sense. It is no use condemning people to slavery in jail where they do not get paid for their work. It would be much better if criminals had to work to pay for their crimes.
I should like this matter to come to a vote. I say to the members of the house that we should give it careful consideration. Now is the time to act if anything is to be done. Were this resolution adopted it would not be necessary to build the $8 million, $20 million or $50 million penitentiaries because criminals-there would be no repeaters-would take care to stay out of jail. Criminals must learn that they must pay for their crimes, and I do not mean in any spiritual sense. They ought to pay in dollars and cents earned by working hard with their hands. The callouses will be there and the electronic machines will see that they do enough work. The computer will see that the mayor's son and the poor boy from the other side of the tracks are treated exactly alike. Criminals cannot stand such treatment. You see, they want justice. There will not be any repeaters.

Mr. Speaker, I think this resolution should be commended to the house for approval. In saying this I certainly do not want to associate myself with some of the remarks made by the hon. member who introduced it.
The proposal, however, to set up a criminal compensation fund for the victims of crime or to set up a criminal injuries compensation board is a sensible, progressive-minded and intelligent one and it should be given full consideration. I should be remiss in my duty if I did not say to the house that to arrive at this conclusion one certainly does not have to support the philosophy pronounced by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan). Indeed, I hasten to say that I repudiate his

philosophy. So far as I understand it, I find it totally repugnant. You do not have to be a retentionist to support this resolution. I know the hon. member's views on this matter, and he is entitled to his views which he expresses with vigour. I respect him for that.
I and many people who believe that the proposal in this resolution is excellent totally disagree with the punitive philosophy which seems to be behind some of the remarks made by the hon. member and which I thought crept into the remarks made by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg). So far as I am concerned, and I think I speak for some others in this house and certainly for those in this party, I am concerned about the criminal, although some people may call it mollycoddling. We know that the so-called criminal is often a victim of circumstances. He is a human being whose problems have to be studied. We do not in the slightest apologize for supporting those aspects of criminal law which in a modern and enlightened age are remedial rather than punitive. We do not dispute the necessity for punishment in the interests of society. The reaction of a barbarous era which fortunately has passed to the modern concept of criminal treatment is to term such treatment "mollycoddling". We want to strike at the roots of crime.
The house may well support this resolution. Our reason for supporting it is that it proposes a social measure of some importance. The modern outlook is that if any member of society is the victim of circumstance, all society should be prepared to bear the burden. The victims of crime are, in effect, victims of society, not only of the individual criminal. This being so, it is a reasonable, sound and forward-looking proposal which the hon. member has made that there should be a fund of the sort suggested.

I adopt the language used at that time. It was pointed out that in England a white paper on compensation for victims of crimes of violence was approved by way of motion on May 5, 1964, by the House of Commons and on May 7 by the House of Lords. A criminal inquiries compensation board was directed to be set up to compensate victims of criminal violence including the spouse or dependants of a person fatally injured. This board operates in much the same manner as does our workmen's compensation board and in the case of a fatal injury any compensation awarded to the spouse or dependants is assessed on the same principles as a claim under the Fatal Accidents Act, except for a restriction in the calculation of the loss of income of the deceased. I believe that New Zealand and California have introduced similar legislation. I agree that Canadians are entitled to ask for precisely similar legislation to be approved here.
There is one aspect of the resolution on which I should like to comment. The last part says that wherever it is possible to do so payment of compensation to those they have injured should be imposed on criminals. I would point out that this is probably a matter for civil law and that at the present time the law provides that if a person injures another by a violent criminal act-and I have no doubt murder would fall into this category under the Fatal Accidents Act-there is a right of civil action for damages against the criminal. The trouble is that most criminals, particularly when they have been executed by due process of law, which happens to a few of them, are not in a good position to pay damages. This is precisely the reason we should set up a criminal injuries compensation board as is proposed in the excellent suggestion before us.
This last part of the proposal is, I believe, unnecessary; it might even be unconstitutional. Nor do I think it would be particularly effective. Certainly if it was designed as extra punishment for those who commit crimes it would in my view be inadequate.

I agree with the intent of the motion now under consideration, partly for the reasons which the hon. member who introduced it has


already advanced. I cannot, however, subscribe to his analogy between the justice of providing compensation for the victims of crime and providing facilities for seeing that justice is done to an accused person. I do not see the validity of this analogy. I am not suggesting that the hon. member put this forward as the basis of his whole argument though in fact a large part of his time was spent in making this comparison.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I have no objection to the state providing facilities to ensure that all reasonable action is taken to see that justice is done to the accused, because until a conviction is handed down we cannot be so presumptuous as to say that the accused is guilty. We may reach such a decision in our minds based on evidence we may have seen, but it is up to the courts to decide whether an accused is guilty and until that decision is handed down we cannot withdraw any of the facilities or money necessary to see that all reasonable action is taken in order that justice may be done to an accused.
Having said that it is also well to say that I do not see any reason why support of this motion should be equated with people who may or may not have supported another measure which was dealt with by the house previously. I believe that is also a false argument so far as support for the motion is concerned. The motion itself is far more adequate to meet the need than the argument advanced by the hon. member who moved it. He based his whole argument on the need for compensation to victims of murder and I do not believe it should be confined to that one kind of crime.
The motion itself refers to victims of crime and I suggest that embraces crimes other than murder. There is need for such a criminal injuries compensation board to look into the matter of compensation for victims of rape, assault and all other crimes of violence.
There may be a right of action under civil law, as suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), so that victims can take an action against a criminal but this is not satisfactory. In most cases the criminals have no funds and it would be an exercise in futility unless there were an unsatisfied judgment fund.
In my province there is such a fund to cover the victims of automobile accidents and most of the money is provided through an extra charge when a licence is purchased.

There would be no similar way to set up such a fund to compensate victims of crime and so it would be necessary for the state to provide the funds.
Then there is the question of administration. I do not know if the hon. member intends that this fund should be operated with the same legal processes as unsatisfied judgment funds. In Alberta there is no way for a victim to get compensation out of the fund unless he first secures an unsatisfied judgment. All the defendant's assets and insurance must first be realized and then the balance is paid from the unsatisfied judgment fund.
References have been made to people being able to collect substantial amounts for slipping on a sidewalk, being caught in a door or injured in an automobile accident in which there was no deliberate criminal intent. The law provides for the collection of such damages but makes no such provision when there is both deliberate and criminal intent.
I have before me some newspaper clippings dealing with people who have been the victims of crime but I shall not take the time to read them into the record. I shall just indicate that there are many cases in which there have been severe miscarriages of justice because the law does not contain any means of providing adequate compensation.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to support the motion and I do not intend to talk it out. During the debate on capital punishment, when I both spoke and voted in favour of abolition, I and others were accused of being more sympathetic to the criminal than to the victim. This was never so. Many of us thought that the abolition of capital punishment would be a step forward in building a more humane and civilized society and would promote an atmosphere in which there would be less violence and crime.
I do not believe that those hon. members who supported abolition were more concerned about the criminal. We were equally concerned about the victim, and right now I give my full support to this motion. As has been mentioned by other hon. members, it seeks to provide compensation for the victims of all crimes, not just murder, but I note that it refers to people who have suffered permanent injury. I would support giving compensation to people who have suffered any type of injury, whether permanent or not, as the result of criminal activity.

I would like to examine the reasons for supporting such a motion. First, I believe the state should compensate the victims of crime because the state did not adequately protect the citizen from the crime. When citizens gave up their right to carry guns to protect themselves they placed their trust in the state to protect them. It is the state's duty to provide adequate police forces and to have control of arms and other dangerous objects, including automobiles. If the state does not do this and the citizen is injured, then the state must bear the consequences.
Second, if the state does not take sufficient measures to prevent criminal behaviour it should also bear the consequences. The state should take measures to see that certain conditions which breed crime are eliminated, conditions such as slums, inadequate housing, inadequate recreation, inadequate education, inadequate opportunities for employment and inadequate family assistance. If the state does not take measures to eliminate these things then the state should compensate the victims of crime to which these things give rise.
Third, and most important, all our Canadian provinces have civil laws which allow the person injured to sue for injuries. He can sue the tort feasor or person who causes the injury, but this is an illusory right of action for the person who is injured in a crime, first, because the criminal is not always caught, second, if he is caught he is often insolvent or has hidden his assets before being caught and, third, if he is caught and convicted he is sent to prison and cannot go to work to pay off the compensation due to the victim.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Compensation boards of this nature are not entirely new to Canada and its provinces. We already have boards and funds, such as the unsatisfied judgment fund, to provide compensation to victims of auto accidents. We have compensation for the families of victims of war and victims of industrial accidents. Other countries already have accepted this idea and have passed legislation to set up such boards. In 1964 New Zealand passed an act to provide compensation for victims of crimes of violence. They established a crimes compensation tribunal to grant expenses incurred as a result of the crime and compensation for any pecuniary loss and for pain and suffering.
In Great Britain they have followed the example of New Zealand. There are several

Criminal Injuries Compensation Board interesting studies which have been proposed. These studies have been referred to by hon. members. One of them is a study published in 1962 by the Conservative party's advisory committee on policy entitled "Victims of Violence". The second was published by the British section of the International Commission of Jurists in their magazine "Justice". It is entitled "Compensation for Victims of Crimes of Violence". Both of these recommended a board to provide such compensation.
Finally, a very interesting book was published in 1960 by Dr. Stephen Schafer at the University of Maryland entitled "Restitution to Victims of Violence". In this book Dr. Schafer makes a comparative study of the laws on this subject in 29 countries. At the time his book was written only Cuba and Switzerland had such funds and boards. He did point out that several countries had a system whereby the criminal could not be granted a suspended sentence or probation unless he guaranteed that the victim of his crime would be compensated. With regard to financing the compensation fund the suggestion found in this book is that the fund should be financed primarily from fines that the state collects in respect of crimes of all types; in other words, the moneys from these fines should go into the fund to pay compensation to the victims injured in crimes. It also is suggested that the board in fact should try to collect from the criminal money or property he may have to help pay the compensation.
I should like to urge the passage of this motion. Such action has been taken in many other countries and I think it would fit into our criminal justice here in Canada.
